title: Who gives a fatwa
hookLine: a mufti gives a non-binding answer to a question

cards: A message sits in a mosque's inbox, typed late at night. Years ago I was sick and missed days of Ramadan. I never made them up.
What do I owe now? No name, maybe. No drama.
Just a person with a question they can't answer alone. Somewhere, someone trained in the law will read it, maybe ask a follow-up, and write back.
That written answer has a name, a word that has picked up a heavy sound in the headlines. Here it means something quieter. A new stretch of the path starts today: law in life.

teach.h: FATWA: AN ANSWER TO A QUESTION.
teach.b: A fatwa is an answer to a question about the law. The one who answers is a mufti. In the Qur'an, people bring questions to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the asking itself is there in the text.
Surah four, near its end, in Pickthall: "They ask thee for a pronouncement. Say: Allah hath pronounced for you concerning distant kindred." Someone asks; an answer comes. Why ask at all?
Surah sixteen says, in Pickthall: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not."

Commentators read it first about the prophets of earlier times, and jurists also drew from it a wider rule: when you don't know, ask someone who does. Now, what a fatwa is not. It is not a court verdict.
A mufti answers the person who asked, about the situation they described. It advises. It doesn't sentence, and it doesn't bind the way a judge's ruling does.
The answer can change if the facts change.
And a mufti is allowed, even expected, to say he doesn't know; the biographies remember Imam Malik answering questions with: I don't know.
Last, the asker still carries something. A man named Wabisa came to the Prophet wanting to ask about righteousness and sin.

In a report in Musnad Ahmad, the Prophet tells him to consult his own heart: righteousness is what the soul is at ease with, and sin is what wavers inside, even if people give you fatwas, and give you fatwas again.
Ask one who knows. Then listen inside, too.

how: Muslims with a question about prayer, fasting, money or family may ask a local imam or a trained mufti, in person, by phone or online; the answer, a fatwa, advises the person who asked and is not a court ruling.

o: an answer to a question about the law, given by a qualified scholar
a formal declaration of war issued by a ruler
a binding court verdict that settles a crime or a dispute

s: a fatwa is a binding verdict, like a court ruling

a good mufti never says I don't know

games.q: you're a mufti. someone asks you a question, and you're not sure of the answer. what do you say?
games.why: the biographies remember Imam Malik answering: I don't know. in this tradition, saying it is part of the job.

practice: Breathe out slowly and find one thing about your practice, your family or your money that you've been guessing about.

Say it to yourself plainly, in one sentence, the way you'd type it into a message, and notice whether it feels heavy or just unfinished. Then let it rest; if you pray, you can ask for a clear answer in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Fatwa. An answer to a question about the law, given by a mufti to the one who asked: advice, not a verdict. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: an answer given by a mufti to a question about the law.

carryVoice: Your line: ask one who knows. A fatwa advises, and the heart still listens. I'll be here tomorrow.
